text:
A: Hello there! Now you must be Lee. I'm Martin. I saw that scarf in your picture, I thought, there's a rugby man.
B: Yeah. Trinity. Wakefield Trinity.
A: League, then. I'm more of a union man myself, Bath mostly, I shout at them on the telly.
B: Union's just people lying in a heap for eighty minutes.
A: No, see, that's not right though, there's a lot of skill in a ruck! Ha, sorry, go on. Where are you, Wakefield?
B: Yeah, Outwood. You?
A: Taunton, Somerset. Cider country. I used to teach geography, so if you ever want to know about the drainage of the Somerset Levels, I'm your man.
B: I'm all right, thanks.
A: Ha! Fair enough, fair enough. Nobody ever does. What do you do yourself?
B: Sales rep, builders' merchants. Timber, sheet materials, all that. I'm out on the road all day, M62 mostly. Sat in traffic, basically.
A: Oh, don't talk to me about roads. The A358 by us has had roadworks on it since about the Romans. Do you enjoy it?
B: It's all right. Good when you close a deal. The admin's a pain, me manager's always chasing me for summat.
A: Ah, admin. That's what did for me in the end, the paperwork. Thirty years teaching and it's the forms that get you, not the kids. I finished a couple of years back. I miss the kids, mind. Not the management.
B: My lad's just started secondary. Year Seven.
A: Has he now? How's he getting on?
B: Says it's fine. That's all I get. Fine. Then he's on FIFA.
A: That's normal, that is, I promise you. Year Sevens are all "fine" till about Christmas. The ones I worried about were the ones that went quiet in a different way, you know, stopped eating their lunch, that sort of thing. If he's coming home and moaning about homework and playing his games, he's doing all right.
B: Yeah. I wonder if I'm strict enough with him, sometimes. It's just me and him, so.
A: Just the two of you? That's hard work.
B: Me mum helps. His mum's in Hull, has him every other weekend. When she can be bothered.
A: Well, I'll tell you something. The kids who did best in my classes weren't the ones with the strictest parents. They were the ones who knew somebody turned up. Every parents' evening, somebody turned up. You sound like you turn up.
B: Yeah. I do, yeah.
A: Sorry, I've gone all teacher on you. My Karen says I can't help it.
B: Nah, it's fine. Makes sense, that.
A: Do you get to the games with him, the rugby?
B: Most home games. He's not that bothered, he comes for the chips.
A: Ha, that's how it starts! My son was the same with cricket, came for the sandwiches, now he's more of a nuisance about it than me. Have you ever been to a County Championship game?
B: Cricket? Nah. Five days of nowt.
A: Four, actually, and it's not nowt! Right, I'm going to have to
